note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Explain how a research project differs from an essay

evidence.title: Essay and project briefs compared against research skill facets
evidence.example: You compare an essay brief with a small research project brief using the six facets of Willison and O'Regan's (2007) Research Skill Development framework, such as embarking and clarifying, finding and generating, and analysing and synthesising. In a short table you show which facets each task stresses, noting that the project asks you to generate your own evidence (for example, an extended project on recycling habits in your college).
evidence.artefact: A comparison table of an essay brief and a project brief against the framework's facets, with a short written explanation.
grounding: model: Research Skill Development framework (Willison and O'Regan 2007)

evidence.title: Annotated summary of a youth club members' survey
evidence.example: You look at a real investigation in a community or workplace setting and explain how it differs from writing an essay (for example, a youth club's survey of members before changing its opening hours). You show that it starts from a question, collects evidence and reports what was found, rather than arguing a case from reading alone.
evidence.artefact: A short annotated summary of the real investigation, labelling its question, evidence and findings, compared with an essay you wrote.
grounding: practice: youth club or community group consultation

genericOutcomes.title: Research project brief compared with an essay brief
genericOutcomes.example: You compare a short research project brief with an essay brief using a recognised framework for research skill development, mapping each task onto stages such as embarking and clarifying, finding and generating, and analysing and synthesising evidence. In a short table you show which stages each task emphasises, noting that the project requires you to generate new evidence rather than build an argument from existing reading alone.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A comparison table setting an essay brief against a project brief using the framework's stages, with a short explanation.
grounding: model: Research Skill Development framework (Willison and O'Regan 2007)

genericOutcomes.title: Annotated summary distinguishing an investigation from an essay
genericOutcomes.example: You look at a real investigation and explain how it differs from writing an essay. You show that it starts from a question, collects evidence systematically, and reports what was found, rather than building a case from reading alone, and you note where the investigation's structure diverges from an essay's structure and why that matters for its findings.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short annotated summary of a real investigation, labelling its question, evidence and findings, compared with an essay.
grounding: professional: Distinguishes a question-led investigation's structure from an argument built solely from reading.

genericOutcomes.title: Research cycle set against essay-based argument
genericOutcomes.example: You set out the stages a piece of research moves through: posing a question, choosing methods to gather evidence, analysing what is found, and reporting it openly, and you contrast this with how an essay is built from existing reading and argument. You identify which stages make a piece of work research rather than commentary, and why each stage affects how trustworthy the findings are.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written comparison setting out the research cycle's stages against how an essay is constructed.
grounding: model: Research Skill Development framework (Willison and O'Regan 2007)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/research-and-enquiry-methods

genericOutcomes.title: Methods and findings explained to someone unfamiliar with research
genericOutcomes.example: You explain to someone unfamiliar with research how a method-based enquiry differs from an opinion piece or essay, covering how the question was chosen, how evidence was gathered and checked, and how findings are reported honestly, including their limits. You show why following a method, rather than only reasoning from what you already believe, changes how trustworthy the conclusions are.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short explanation, written for a non-specialist, of how a method-based enquiry differs from an argued essay.
grounding: professional: Explains how evidence gathered through a defined method differs from opinion or argument alone.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/research-and-enquiry-methods

capabilities.statement: Formulate a research question, rationale and aims

evidence.title: Proposal outline annotated against the embark and clarify facet
evidence.example: You draft a research question, rationale and aims for a first proposal, working through the embark and clarify facet of Willison and O'Regan's (2007) Research Skill Development framework, which is about working out what knowledge is needed and why. You annotate how your rationale shows the need and how each aim follows from the question (for example, a history proposal on how local newspapers reported the 1926 General Strike).
evidence.artefact: A one-page proposal outline with question, rationale and aims, annotated against the embark and clarify facet.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007

evidence.title: Agreed research brief for a local gym
evidence.example: You define a question for a real client need, with its purpose and scope (for example, a business student on a live brief who turns a local gym's worry about losing members into a question about why new members cancel within three months, with aims agreed with the manager). You show how the client's need, not just your interest, shaped the question.
evidence.artefact: The agreed research brief showing the question, purpose, scope and aims, with the client's email confirming them.
grounding: professional: Defines a research or evaluation question for a client or policy need, with its purpose and scope.
professional: GSR technical framework: identifying research needs, designing and specifying research

genericOutcomes.title: Proposal outline annotated against a research skill facet
genericOutcomes.example: You draft a research question, rationale and aims for a first proposal, working through a stage of a recognised research skill development framework concerned with working out what knowledge is needed and why. You annotate how your rationale demonstrates that need and how each aim follows logically from the question, checking that nothing in the aims goes beyond what the question actually asks.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A one-page proposal outline with question, rationale and aims, annotated against the framework's relevant stage.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007

genericOutcomes.title: Research brief agreed to meet a defined need
genericOutcomes.example: You define a question for a real need, setting out its purpose and scope, then turn a stated worry or problem into a specific question with aims that are agreed by whoever holds the need. You show how the need itself, not just your own interest, shaped the question, and you record the agreement in writing before moving on.
genericOutcomes.artefact: The agreed research brief showing the question, purpose, scope and aims, with written confirmation that it was agreed.
grounding: professional: Defines a research or evaluation question for a stated need, with its purpose and scope.

genericOutcomes.title: Hypothesis and question generated from a problem area
genericOutcomes.example: Starting from a broad problem area, you generate a testable question or hypothesis, then set out the rationale for why it matters and the specific aims that will answer it. You check that each aim is something you can actually achieve with the time and evidence available, and you revise the question until rationale and aims line up with each other.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A worked example moving from a broad problem to a question, rationale and aims, with revision notes.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/3.16

genericOutcomes.title: Question and aims specified for a commissioned enquiry
genericOutcomes.example: You are asked to scope a piece of work and must generate a workable question from a general concern, then state why it matters and what the aims will deliver. You check the question is something that can genuinely be explored with the resources available, and you set out aims that a commissioner could check progress against.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A specification document stating the question, rationale and aims, checked against the resources available.
grounding: professional: Defines a research or evaluation question for a client or policy need, with its purpose and scope.
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/3.16

capabilities.statement: Narrow a topic to a question one can research

evidence.title: PICO worksheet narrowing a broad topic
evidence.example: You narrow a broad topic to a question you can answer by applying the PICO framework (Richardson et al. 1995): population, intervention, comparison and outcome. You show each step from topic to question and note what you left out and why, recognising the limits of what you can research in the time available (for example, a physiotherapy student narrowing exercise and back pain to one adult group and one outcome).
evidence.artefact: A topic-narrowing worksheet showing successive versions of the question, the PICO breakdown and your reasons for each cut.
grounding: model: PICO question framework (Richardson et al. 1995)

evidence.title: Scoped question agreed with a river trust coordinator
evidence.example: You narrow a broad question from a real setting to one you can answer with the time and access you have (for example, a geography student volunteering with a river trust who turns plastic pollution in the river into a question about litter counts at three sites over six weeks). You discuss the scope with the volunteer coordinator and record what you decided not to cover.
evidence.artefact: Notes from the scoping conversation and the final question, with a list of what was left out and why.
grounding: practice: environmental charity volunteering

genericOutcomes.title: Broad topic narrowed using a structured question framework
genericOutcomes.example: You narrow a broad topic to a question you can actually answer by applying a structured framework that breaks a question into its population, intervention or focus, comparison and outcome. You show each step from topic to question and note what you deliberately left out and why, recognising the limits of what can be researched in the time available.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A topic-narrowing worksheet showing successive versions of the question, the framework's breakdown and your reasons for each cut.
grounding: model: PICO question framework (Richardson et al. 1995)

genericOutcomes.title: Scoped question agreed within real time and access limits
genericOutcomes.example: You narrow a broad question from a real setting to one you can answer with the time and access you actually have, turning a general concern into something specific and measurable. You discuss the scope with whoever holds the setting, agree what is realistic, and record in writing what you decided not to cover and why.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Notes from the scoping conversation and the final question, with a list of what was left out and why.
grounding: professional: Negotiates the scope of an enquiry against the time and access actually available.

genericOutcomes.title: Testable question generated and refined from a broad area
genericOutcomes.example: You take a broad area of interest and generate a series of increasingly specific, testable questions, checking each one against what evidence would actually be needed to answer it. You refine the question until it is narrow enough to investigate properly, keeping a record of each version and the reason for narrowing it further.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A sequence of question versions from broad to specific, each annotated with the reason for narrowing it.
grounding: model: PICO question framework (Richardson et al. 1995)
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/3.16

genericOutcomes.title: Enquiry scoped to fit real constraints on time and access
genericOutcomes.example: Given a broad concern and limited time, you generate a specific question that can realistically be explored with the access and resources you have. You check the question against what data collection would actually require, negotiate scope with whoever controls access, and document what has been excluded from the final enquiry and why.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A scoping document recording the narrowed question, the constraints considered and what was excluded.
grounding: professional: Negotiates the scope of an enquiry against the time and access actually available.
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/3.16

capabilities.statement: Structure and write a literature review and a research report

evidence.title: Thematic literature review and structured report draft
evidence.example: You write a short literature review and a project report, using the analyse and synthesise and the communicate and apply facets of Willison and O'Regan's (2007) Research Skill Development framework to check each part. You show that the review groups sources by theme and critiques them rather than summarising one at a time, and that the report follows a clear structure (for example, an education report on homework policy with introduction, method, results and discussion).
evidence.artefact: A literature review and report draft, annotated to show synthesis across sources and the purpose of each report section.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007

evidence.title: Evidence review with executive summary for councillors
evidence.example: You review existing evidence and report findings for people who need to act on them (for example, a public health student on placement with a local council producing a short evidence review on active travel schemes, with an executive summary for councillors). You choose a structure that suits busy readers while keeping the review accurate and properly sourced.
evidence.artefact: The evidence review and report with its executive summary, and feedback from the placement supervisor on its usefulness.
grounding: professional: Reviews existing evidence and reports findings for decision-makers.
professional: GSR technical framework: analysis and interpretation; leading, communicating and championing social research

genericOutcomes.title: Literature review and report draft checked against two facets
genericOutcomes.example: You write a short literature review and a project report, using two stages of a recognised research skill framework, one concerned with analysing and synthesising sources and the other with communicating findings clearly, to check each part. You show that the review groups sources by theme and critiques them rather than summarising one at a time, and that the report follows a clear, logical structure.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A literature review and report draft, annotated to show synthesis across sources and the purpose of each section.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007

genericOutcomes.title: Evidence review with an executive summary for decision-makers
genericOutcomes.example: You review existing evidence and report findings for people who need to act on them, producing a short evidence review with an executive summary aimed at busy readers. You choose a structure that suits those readers while keeping the review accurate and properly sourced, and you check the summary still reflects the full review's conclusions fairly.
genericOutcomes.artefact: The evidence review and report with its executive summary, and feedback on its usefulness for decision-making.
grounding: professional: Reviews existing evidence and reports findings for decision-makers.

genericOutcomes.title: Empirical findings reported through a structured report format
genericOutcomes.example: You conduct a small piece of empirical research and report it using a standard structure covering introduction, method, results and discussion, checking that each section does only the job it is meant to do. You write a literature review beforehand that groups existing studies by theme rather than listing them, so the report's introduction can justify the study clearly.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A structured empirical report with a preceding literature review, each section checked against its intended purpose.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/3.18

genericOutcomes.title: Empirical findings reported for a non-specialist audience
genericOutcomes.example: You conduct and report a small piece of empirical work for an audience that did not run the study, structuring the report so the method and results are clear even to someone unfamiliar with the detail. You write a short preceding review of existing evidence so the reader understands why the question mattered before seeing your own findings.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A structured empirical report with a preceding evidence review, written for a non-specialist audience.
grounding: professional: Reviews existing evidence and reports findings for decision-makers.
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/3.18

capabilities.statement: Write a research proposal that answers each of its questions

evidence.title: Full proposal checked section by section for workability
evidence.example: You write a full research proposal and check that each section answers its question: what you will study, why, how, when and with what resources. You use the organise and manage facet of Willison and O'Regan's (2007) Research Skill Development framework to test whether your plan, timeline and methods are workable, and revise weak sections (for example, a criminology proposal on how young people perceive stop and search).
evidence.artefact: A complete research proposal with a checklist mapping each section to the question it answers, and a revision log.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007

evidence.title: Survey bid for a local wildlife trust
evidence.example: You write a short bid or specification for a real commissioner (for example, an environmental science student responding to a local wildlife trust's call for a small hedgehog survey, setting out the question, method, outputs, timescale and costs). You decide what can realistically be delivered and justify those choices to the funder.
evidence.artefact: The submitted bid or specification, with the commissioner's response or written feedback on it.
grounding: professional: Writes a research specification or bid that sets out the question, method, outputs and plan.
professional: Vitae RDF C2 Research management: research strategy

genericOutcomes.title: Full proposal checked section by section for workability
genericOutcomes.example: You write a full research proposal and check that each section answers its own question: what you will study, why, how, when and with what resources. You use a stage of a recognised research skill framework concerned with organising and managing a project to test whether your plan, timeline and methods are actually workable, and you revise any weak sections you find.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A complete research proposal with a checklist mapping each section to the question it answers, and a revision log.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007

genericOutcomes.title: Bid or specification written for a real commissioner
genericOutcomes.example: You write a short bid or specification for a real commissioner, setting out the question, method, outputs, timescale and costs for a piece of work someone else needs done. You decide what can realistically be delivered within the time and budget on offer, and you justify those choices clearly to whoever will decide whether to fund the work.
genericOutcomes.artefact: The submitted bid or specification, with the commissioner's response or written feedback on it.
grounding: professional: Writes a research specification or bid that sets out the question, method, outputs and plan.

genericOutcomes.title: Proposal sections tested against the methods they rely on
genericOutcomes.example: You write a research proposal and check that its chosen methods of enquiry can actually answer the question it sets, testing each section, question, method, timeline and resourcing, against what the evidence will need to show. Where a section's method would not generate evidence strong enough to answer its question, you revise the method rather than the question.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A proposal with each section tested against the evidence its chosen method could realistically produce.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/research-and-enquiry-methods

genericOutcomes.title: Proposal defended against questions about its own methods
genericOutcomes.example: You write a proposal for a piece of work and prepare to defend it against questions about whether its methods of enquiry will actually answer what it sets out to answer. For each section you can state the method used, why it suits the question, and what evidence it will produce, so a reviewer can check the plan holds together before any work begins.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A proposal document with a short defence note explaining why each method fits the question it answers.
grounding: professional: Writes a research specification or bid that sets out the question, method, outputs and plan.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/research-and-enquiry-methods

capabilities.statement: Review the literature as critique, to place own research in it

evidence.title: Literature review opening structured with the CARS moves
evidence.example: You structure the opening of your literature review using Swales' (1990) Create a Research Space model: establish the territory, establish a niche by showing a gap or problem in existing studies, and occupy the niche with your own study. You critique key studies' methods and limits to show why your project is needed (for example, a marketing dissertation showing that research on trust in influencers rarely covers older consumers).
evidence.artefact: A literature review section annotated with the three moves, showing where critique of earlier studies creates the gap.
grounding: model: Create a Research Space (CARS) model (Swales 1990)

evidence.title: Positioning note building on earlier accessibility audits
evidence.example: In a work or community project, you review what has already been done and show how your work adds to it (for example, a computing student on placement who reviews earlier accessibility audits of the company's app, identifies what they missed, and positions their own user testing to fill that gap). You critique the earlier work fairly and use it to justify your approach.
evidence.artefact: A short positioning paper or project initiation note summarising prior work, its limits and how your project builds on it.
grounding: practice: industry placement project

genericOutcomes.title: Literature review opening structured through three established moves
genericOutcomes.example: You structure the opening of your literature review using an established model for creating a research space: establishing the territory, establishing a niche by showing a gap or problem in existing studies, and occupying that niche with your own study. You critique key studies' methods and limits honestly, to show why your own project is needed rather than merely interesting.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A literature review section annotated with the three moves, showing where critique of earlier studies creates the gap.
grounding: model: Create a Research Space (CARS) model (Swales 1990)

genericOutcomes.title: Positioning note building on prior work's limits
genericOutcomes.example: In a real project, you review what has already been done and show how your own work adds to it, identifying what earlier work missed or left unresolved and positioning your own enquiry to fill that specific gap. You critique the earlier work fairly rather than dismissing it, and you use its limits to justify the approach you are taking.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short positioning note summarising prior work, its limits and how your own project builds on it.
grounding: professional: Reviews prior work fairly and positions a new piece of enquiry against its identified gaps.

genericOutcomes.title: Own enquiry positioned against existing methods of research
genericOutcomes.example: You review how previous work in your area has approached its questions, examining the methods of enquiry used and where they fall short, then use that critique to justify the specific approach your own research takes. You show that your project is not simply repeating earlier work but responding directly to a gap or weakness you have identified in it.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written critique of existing approaches that justifies the specific method chosen for your own enquiry.
grounding: model: Create a Research Space (CARS) model (Swales 1990)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/research-and-enquiry-methods

genericOutcomes.title: New work positioned against the limits of earlier enquiry
genericOutcomes.example: Before starting a piece of work, you review the methods and findings of enquiries that came before it, identify where their approach fell short or left questions open, and position your own work to address that specific limitation. You present this positioning clearly enough that someone reviewing your plan can see exactly what gap it is meant to close.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A positioning brief identifying limits in prior enquiry and how the current work responds to them.
grounding: professional: Reviews prior work fairly and positions a new piece of enquiry against its identified gaps.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/research-and-enquiry-methods

capabilities.statement: Apply research ethics, including consent and anonymisation

evidence.title: Ethics application for an interview study with carers
evidence.example: You prepare an ethics application for a study with human participants, applying the ESRC research ethics principles to consent, anonymisation and data storage. You use the levels of student autonomy in Willison and O'Regan's (2007) Research Skill Development framework to show you are making these decisions yourself rather than following set steps (for example, a nursing study interviewing family carers, with a consent form, a right to withdraw and a plan to remove identifying details).
evidence.artefact: Your ethics application, participant information sheet, consent form and anonymisation plan, with the panel's approval or requested changes.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007
model: ESRC Framework for Research Ethics (ESRC 2015)

evidence.title: Ethics decision record for a youth academy sleep survey
evidence.example: You run research within an organisation's ethics and data protection rules (for example, a sport science student on placement with a football academy surveying players' sleep, who checks the plan with the club's safeguarding lead and data protection officer because some players are under 18). You record each ethical decision and why you made it, and report results so no individual can be identified.
evidence.artefact: A decision record of ethical and data protection choices, with the data protection officer's sign-off and the anonymised report.
grounding: professional: Conducts research within an employer's or funder's ethics and data protection requirements.
professional: Vitae RDF C1 Professional conduct: ethics, principles and sustainability; legal requirements

genericOutcomes.title: Ethics application drafted for a study with human participants
genericOutcomes.example: You prepare an ethics application for a study involving human participants, applying established research ethics principles to consent, anonymisation and data storage. You use a recognised scale of researcher independence to show that you are making these decisions yourself, with reasons, rather than simply following a fixed checklist handed to you by someone else.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Your ethics application, participant information sheet, consent form and anonymisation plan, with any requested changes recorded.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007
model: ESRC Framework for Research Ethics (ESRC 2015)

genericOutcomes.title: Ethics decision record kept for a real piece of research
genericOutcomes.example: You run a piece of research within an organisation's ethics and data protection rules, checking your plan with whoever is responsible for safeguarding and data protection before collecting anything, especially where participants might be vulnerable. You record each ethical decision and the reason behind it, and you report results so that no individual participant can be identified.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A decision record of ethical and data protection choices, with sign-off and the anonymised final report.
grounding: professional: Conducts research within an employer's or funder's ethics and data protection requirements.

genericOutcomes.title: Ethical issues identified and resolved before data collection
genericOutcomes.example: Before collecting any data, you identify the ethical issues your study raises, consent, anonymisation, storage and the risk of harm, and you set out how each will be handled and why that handling is appropriate. You treat this as a reasoned judgement you are responsible for, not a form to complete, and you can explain each decision if challenged.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written ethical risk assessment identifying each issue raised and the reasoned response to it.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007
model: ESRC Framework for Research Ethics (ESRC 2015)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/ethics

genericOutcomes.title: Ethical responsibilities acted on throughout a piece of work
genericOutcomes.example: Throughout a piece of work involving other people's data or participation, you act on your ethical responsibilities rather than treating them as a one-off approval step, checking consent remains valid, anonymisation holds, and storage stays secure as the work progresses. You can point to specific moments where you changed your approach because of an ethical concern you noticed.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A log of ethical checks made during the work, with at least one documented change made in response.
grounding: professional: Conducts research within an employer's or funder's ethics and data protection requirements.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/ethics

capabilities.statement: Choose and justify a methodology and methods for a question

evidence.title: Methodology section justified layer by layer
evidence.example: You justify your methodology using the research onion (Saunders, Lewis and Thornhill 2019), working through its layers from research philosophy and approach to methodological choice, strategy, time horizon and techniques. You link each choice to your question, and use the find and generate facet of Willison and O'Regan's (2007) Research Skill Development framework to show how your methods will produce the evidence needed (for example, a psychology project choosing mixed methods).
evidence.artefact: A methodology section with a diagram of your choice at each layer and a written justification for each.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007
model: Research onion (Saunders, Lewis and Thornhill 2019)

evidence.title: Methods options paper for a junction congestion study
evidence.example: You select and defend methods for a real project with limits on time, cost and access (for example, a civil engineering student on placement choosing between new traffic counts and existing sensor data to assess congestion at a junction, and explaining the trade-offs to the project lead). You show that your choice fits the question and the decision the evidence will serve.
evidence.artefact: A methods options paper comparing approaches against the question and constraints, with the project lead's decision recorded.
grounding: professional: Selects and defends research methods that fit the question, the evidence needed and the constraints.
professional: GSR technical framework: knowledge of research methods; identifying research needs, designing and specifying research

genericOutcomes.title: Methodology justified through a layered decision model
genericOutcomes.example: You justify your methodology using a recognised layered model of research design, working through its layers from research philosophy and approach to methodological choice, strategy, time horizon and techniques. You link each layer's choice directly to your question, checking that the methods you select will actually produce the kind of evidence the question needs.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A methodology section with a diagram of your choice at each layer and a written justification for each.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007
model: Research onion (Saunders, Lewis and Thornhill 2019)

genericOutcomes.title: Methods compared and defended within real constraints
genericOutcomes.example: You select and defend methods for a real project where time, cost and access are all limited, comparing two or more realistic options against what each would actually tell you. You explain the trade-offs of each option to whoever will use the findings, and you show that your final choice fits both the question and the decision the evidence needs to support.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A methods options paper comparing approaches against the question and constraints, with the final decision recorded.
grounding: professional: Selects and defends research methods that fit the question, the evidence needed and the constraints.

genericOutcomes.title: Qualitative, quantitative or mixed methods chosen for fit
genericOutcomes.example: Facing a research question, you consider qualitative, quantitative and mixed methods in turn and choose whichever combination actually fits the question, rather than defaulting to the method you find most familiar or comfortable. You justify the choice by explaining what kind of evidence each option would produce and why that evidence answers the question better than the alternatives.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written justification comparing qualitative, quantitative and mixed options against the research question.
grounding: ing:doc:research-skill-development-willison-2007
model: Research onion (Saunders, Lewis and Thornhill 2019)
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/3.6

genericOutcomes.title: Appropriate methods chosen and defended for a live question
genericOutcomes.example: Given a live question that needs answering, you weigh qualitative, quantitative and mixed approaches against what is actually achievable and what evidence each would yield, then choose and defend the combination that best fits the question rather than the easiest option available. You present this justification clearly enough for someone else to check your reasoning before work begins.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A methods justification document comparing qualitative, quantitative and mixed options against the live question.
grounding: professional: Selects and defends research methods that fit the question, the evidence needed and the constraints.
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/3.6

genericOutcomes.title: Dissertation plan built with scope, milestones and risks
genericOutcomes.example: You scope and plan an extended, independent piece of research at a stage of a recognised autonomy framework where you set the question and methods yourself, rather than following a set brief. You produce a plan with milestones, risks and fallback options, and you justify in writing what is deliberately in scope and what is left out.

genericOutcomes.title: Extended project planned and managed within a fixed budget
genericOutcomes.example: You plan and manage an extended research project for an organisation, working within a fixed budget and a deadline set by an external event. You agree the project's scope with the people who hold a stake in it, track progress against the plan, and renegotiate that scope openly whenever a new risk makes the original plan unworkable.
genericOutcomes.artefact: The project plan, budget tracker and progress reports, with a stakeholder note on delivery against the agreed scope.
grounding: professional: Plans and manages a research project to time, scope and budget.

genericOutcomes.title: Extended enquiry scoped around its own methods of research
genericOutcomes.example: You plan an extended piece of research by first deciding which methods of enquiry the project will use, then scoping the work's size, timeline and resourcing around what those methods can realistically deliver. You set milestones tied to each stage of the method, and you build in fallback options for stages most likely to run into difficulty or delay.
genericOutcomes.artefact: An extended project plan with milestones tied to each stage of the chosen method, including fallback options.

genericOutcomes.title: Large-scale enquiry planned around realistic delivery constraints
genericOutcomes.example: You are responsible for planning a large, independent piece of enquiry and must scope its methods of research against what time, budget and access will realistically allow before committing to a plan.
